item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports testing history dependence directly. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) reports that excessive emphasis on recent interactions can harm recommendation accuracy; greater recency sensitivity is therefore not automatically desirable. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) uses genetic algorithms to find minimal history edits that change recommendations, providing a concrete precedent for perturbation probes. [Stability-aware Preference Modeling (2025)](https://cis.temple.edu/~jiewu/research/publications/Publication_files/2025-TWeb-Stability-aware%20Preference%20Modeling%20for%20Sequential%20Recommendation.pdf) separates long- and short-term interests and models interaction stability, motivating diagnostics across different history lengths and temporal patterns.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: compare intact histories against equal-sized recent-item and older-item removals, shuffled histories, and shuffling that preserves the last item. Keep candidate sets fixed; report top-10 overlap, target-rank changes, and validation HR@10 differences by dataset and history-length bucket. Separate deletion effects from positional shifts through matched masking and compacted-history controls. For architectures with explicit aggregation branches, compare learned aggregation with uniform pooling, last-item-only scoring, and disabling the history residual; measure changes in scores and rankings rather than treating residual magnitude alone as contribution. These are proposed probes, not established findings from the cited papers. Sensitivity demonstrates model dependence on the manipulated input or component; it does not establish actual user intent, causal preference drift, or the irrelevance of older interactions."}
